summary: Describes a method for identifying flows or flow groups within pseudowires so MPLS routers can spread them over equal-cost paths. Forwarding engines normally hash the MPLS label stack to balance load, so without flow identification a pseudowire would use only one path.

eli5.summary: Many lanes of a highway help only if cars are spread over them. This adds a small tag to each flow inside a pseudowire so routers can share the load across lanes.

subtitle: Adds a flow label to pseudowire packets so MPLS routers can spread traffic across equal-cost paths.

tldr.problem: A pseudowire normally rides a single network path, and routers in the middle cannot see the flows inside it. A busy pseudowire therefore cannot use the equal-cost paths that exist.
tldr.mechanism: The ingress edge router adds one extra MPLS label, the flow label, at the bottom of the label stack. All packets of one flow get the same label, so routers can hash it to pick a path. The egress router discards it.
tldr.outcome: Flows inside a pseudowire can be balanced over equal-cost paths, but packet order is kept only within a flow. RFC 6391 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 7274.

facts.label: Traffic Class field
facts.value: Set to zero, ignored on receipt

today: RFC 6391 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 7274. The text itself describes the flow label as an OPTIONAL mode, with single-path transport remaining the default.

sections.title: Why Pseudowires Use One Path
sections.content:
A pseudowire (PW) is normally carried over a single network path, even when several Equal Cost Multiple Paths (ECMPs) exist between the two provider edge (PE) routers. That keeps the emulated service in order. Using one path stays the default.

Some PWs carry large volumes of IP traffic between routers, from hundreds of Mbps to Gbps. They only need order preserved inside each IP flow, not between all flows. Spreading many small flows over several paths also makes capacity planning easier.

The problem is visibility. A router in the middle cannot tell what kind of PW it is forwarding, so it can only hash the MPLS label stack, which is too coarse. The ingress PE can see the packet headers, so it adds a label chosen by itself. The RFC calls this mode OPTIONAL and says it should be used only when ECMP is known to help the PW.
sections.eli5: All the toy trucks from one factory are told to use the same road, even though there are several roads. The factory knows what is in each truck, so it can add a tag so the crossroads can split them up.

sections.title: The Flow Label
sections.content:
The design adds one more MPLS label stack entry, the flow LSE, between the PW label entry and the control word (or between the PW entry and the payload if there is no control word). The label it carries is the flow label.

The ingress PE MUST map indivisible flows to the same flow label. The label MUST NOT be a reserved MPLS label (values 0 to 15), and it SHOULD stay constant for the life of the flow. The RFC recommends generating values with a high degree of entropy so routers spread flows evenly. How the values are chosen is outside its scope.

At the egress PE the flow LSE is discarded without processing, unless it carries a reserved label, in which case that label's rules apply. The TTL of the flow LSE is advised to be 1, so a packet is dropped if the flow LSE ever ends up on top of the stack by mistake. The Traffic Class field MUST be set to zero and ignored on receipt.

Another way to balance load, creating several PWs and sharing flows among them, was considered and rejected. It adds less entropy and needs more PWs to be set up and maintained.
sections.eli5: The sender sticks a random-looking number on every package from the same customer. Roads in the middle look at the number to choose a lane, and the receiver peels the sticker off.

sections.title: Where Flows Come From and How Packets Are Built
sections.content:
The Native Service Processing (NSP) function in the ingress PE is REQUIRED to identify flows or groups of flows and tell the PW forwarder which flow each packet belongs to. For an Ethernet PW, the NSP might treat all packets with the same source and destination address pair as one indivisible flow. How flows are identified is outside the scope of the RFC.

The encapsulation, from the payload down, is: the payload, an optional control word (4 octets), the flow LSE (4 octets), the PW LSE (4 octets), and then the MPLS tunnel LSEs at four octets each. The ingress PE adds the control word if it applies, then pushes the flow label, then the PW label.
sections.eli5: A helper looks at each package and decides which pile it belongs to. Then the package gets its pile number tag, its delivery tag and its road tags, in that order.

sections.title: Signalling the Flow Label
sections.content:
With LDP-based PW signalling from RFC 4447, a new interface parameter, the Flow Label Sub-TLV, tells the two PEs whether flow labels are in use. Its identifier is 0x17, its length is 4 and it carries two bits: T (the PE wants to send a flow label) and R (the PE can receive one). The remaining bits are reserved, set to zero and ignored on receipt.

A PE includes a flow label only when it sent T = 1 and received R = 1 from its peer. In every other case, including when no Sub-TLV is received, it MUST NOT include one. Unknown interface parameters are silently ignored, so older implementations are unaffected. Only the wish to use a flow LSE is signalled. The label value stays a local matter of the ingress PE.

The two directions are independent, so asymmetric operation is allowed. For static pseudowires without signalling, both ends must be provisioned identically, and the default is not to use the flow label. Multi-segment PWs work without changes to the switching PEs.
sections.eli5: Before using the stickers, each side raises a hand to say whether it will send them and whether it can read them. Stickers are used only if one side sends and the other reads.

sections.title: OAM and Troubleshooting
sections.content:
Load balancing complicates testing. For a basic check that the PW is configured, a Virtual Circuit Connectivity Verification (VCCV) message may be sent with any flow label value. To prove the PW works for all flows, a VCCV message MUST be sent over each ECMP path, which the RFC notes may be difficult and scales poorly.

The RFC argues that sending over one path may be enough, because the network's own IGP failure detection and convergence normally repairs failures in the packet switched network. A corrupted forwarding entry in one router would only be found if the test happens to take that path. For out-of-band VCCV, a Router Alert label is added to the stack, which may send the OAM packet down a different path from the data packets.
sections.eli5: If you want to be sure every lane of the road is open, you have to send a test car down each lane. Sending only one test car might miss a pothole in another lane.

sections.title: When It Helps and When It Does Not
sections.content:
The mechanism helps most when a PE can tell flows apart and the PW's access speed is large compared with the core link bandwidth (the RFC gives 10% or more as an example). It focuses on Ethernet. It also works for link bundles, Link Aggregation Groups and multiple RSVP-TE paths. Core routers need no new capability.

Order is kept only within a flow. If sequence number support is needed, the flow label mechanism MUST NOT be used. Ethernet control frames SHOULD always use the same path. It MUST NOT be deployed in an MPLS-TP network unless the service's integrity requirements can still be met.

If one big flow dominates, as with a single large TCP flow or encrypted flows the PE cannot separate, there is no benefit. The operator can do nothing, police flow bandwidth, give high-bandwidth flows a constant label, or give them random labels at the cost of out-of-order traffic. Customers can also split traffic into more flows, for example with parallel TCP sessions.
sections.eli5: Splitting packages across lanes only helps if there are lots of small packages. One giant package still has to go down a single lane.

sections.title: Security, IANA and Congestion
sections.content:
The general PW security considerations of RFC 3985 and those of the specific PW type apply, as do those of RFC 5920. The TTL of 1 on the flow LSE prevents accidental forwarding of a packet based on the flow label.

IANA registered the Flow Label Sub-TLV type 0x17 (length 4) in the Pseudowire Interface Parameters Sub-TLV type registry. For congestion, the considerations of RFC 3985 apply. If only IP packets are classified into flows, their normal congestion behaviour is enough. For non-IP flows, PW congestion avoidance must be applied to each load balance group.
sections.eli5: The little tag is set up so that, if it is ever by mistake on top, the packet is thrown away instead of being sent off to the wrong place.
